title: Fewest Lane Changes Past the Cones
statement:
A runner moves along a road with three lanes, numbered 1 to 3, from point 0 to point n. They start at point 0 in lane 2.

The array cones has length n + 1. If cones[i] is 1, 2 or 3, there is a cone at point i in that lane. If it is 0, point i is clear. There is at most one cone per point, and points 0 and n are always clear.

From point i the runner can step forward to point i + 1 in the same lane, but only if that spot has no cone. At any point they can also change to any other lane at the same point (a jump from lane 1 to lane 3 is one change), but only into a spot without a cone.

Return the smallest number of lane changes needed to reach point n in any lane.

examples.why: Lane 2 is blocked at point 1. Changing to lane 1 would hit the cone at point 3 and cost a second change; lane 3 is clear all the way.
No cone is ever in lane 2, so the runner never changes.
At point 1 change to lane 3, run to point 2, then change to lane 1 and run to the end.

hints: At each point you only need to know one number per lane: the fewest changes needed to stand there.
Moving to the next point is free in every lane without a cone. A lane with a cone at that point becomes unreachable.
After moving forward, any lane can also be reached from the best other lane for one extra change: best[j] = min(best[j], min(best) + 1), as long as lane j has no cone at this point.

explain.intuition:
Keep three numbers: best[lane] is the fewest changes to be at the current point in that lane. Before the run starts, lane 2 costs 0 and the other two cost 1 (change at point 0).

Advance one point at a time. Stepping forward costs nothing, so the numbers carry over, except the lane with a cone, which becomes infinity. Then every clear lane can also be reached by one change from the cheapest lane at this point: min(best) + 1. Three numbers per point, so the whole road is O(n). Picking the "obvious" free lane is not enough: in the first example lane 1 looks fine at point 1 but runs into a cone two points later.
steps: For each point i from 1 to n: if cones[i] > 0, set that lane's value to infinity.
Let m = min(best). For every lane without a cone at i, set best[lane] = min(best[lane], m + 1).
pitfalls: Changing lanes into a spot that has a cone. The relax step must skip the blocked lane, or it gets m + 1 back.
Greedily switching to the first free lane. It can lead into a cone soon after, as in the first example.
Charging two changes for a jump from lane 1 to lane 3. Any lane change costs one.

solutions.title: 0-1 BFS over (point, lane)
solutions.idea: Each state is a point and a lane. Moving forward costs 0, changing lanes costs 1. A deque processes 0-cost moves first, which gives shortest distances without a heap.

solutions.title: Three running costs
solutions.idea: Carry the fewest changes per lane forward one point at a time; block the coned lane, then let clear lanes take min + 1.

followups: The road has k lanes and a point can hold several cones. How does the cost of each step change?
Also return the sequence of lanes the runner uses. What would you store to rebuild it?
